title: Functorial injective resolutions preserving lower bounds
statement: Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category [def-sp-abelian] equipped with functorial injective embeddings: a functor $J:\mathcal A\to\mathcal A$ and a natural monomorphism $\mathrm{id}\to J$, with every $J(A)$ injective [def-sp-injective-resolutions]. On the category of bounded-below integer-indexed cochain complexes [def-weil-abstract-derived-category], there exist a functor $I$ and a natural quasi-isomorphism $K\to I(K)$ such that every term of $I(K)$ is injective and, for every integer $a$, if $K^n=0$ for all $n<a$, then $I(K)^n=0$ for all $n<a$. The same functor $I$ works for all lower bounds and all diagrams of bounded-below complexes.

source.place: Tag 0141 (lemma-functorial-injective-resolutions), assertion (1) and its construction with J(0)=0 and I^{p,q}=0 for p<a or q<0

proof.text: Normalize the supplied embedding once, independently of any complex. Put $r_A=J(A\to0)$ and $s_A=J(0\to A)$, so $r_As_A=1$. Put $J_0(A)=\ker r_A$ with inclusion $k_A$. The morphism $1-s_Ar_A$ factors through $k_A$, giving $t_A:J(A)\to J_0(A)$ with $k_At_A=1-s_Ar_A$. Since $r_Ak_A=0$, we have $k_At_Ak_A=k_A$; cancellation of the monomorphism $k_A$ gives $t_Ak_A=1$. Naturality gives $r_A\eta_A=\eta_0(A\to0)=0$, so $\eta_A$ factors uniquely as $k_A\eta^0_A$ and $\eta^0_A$ is monic. For $f:A\to B$, the identity $r_BJ(f)=r_A$ gives the unique induced map $J_0(f)$ on kernels. Kernel uniqueness proves identity, composition and naturality of $\eta^0$. This uses kernels and the zero object of [def-sp-abelian].

Each $J_0(A)$ is injective by [def-sp-injective-resolutions]: for a monomorphism $M\to N$ and a map $M\to J_0(A)$, compose with $k_A$, extend to $N\to J(A)$ by the given injectivity, and compose with $t_A$. The composite extends the original map since $t_Ak_A=1$. Also $J_0(0)=\ker(1_{J(0)})$ is a zero object. Consequently $J_0$ sends every zero morphism to zero: factor a zero morphism through the zero object and use that $J_0(0)$ is zero. No additivity of $J$ or $J_0$ is asserted or needed.

source.place: Tag 0141 (lemma-functorial-injective-resolutions), proof, normalization and preservation of zero morphisms

proof.text: Fix kernels and cokernels throughout. Recursively define object functors $Q_0=\mathrm{id}$, $E_q=J_0Q_q$, and $Q_{q+1}(A)=\operatorname{coker}(\eta^0_{Q_q(A)})$ for $q\ge0$, with quotient $\pi_{q,A}:E_q(A)\to Q_{q+1}(A)$. For $f:A\to B$, define $Q_{q+1}(f)$ by $Q_{q+1}(f)\pi_{q,A}=\pi_{q,B}E_q(f)$. Naturality of $\eta^0$ proves existence; uniqueness against the cokernel quotient proves preservation of identities and composition. Induction shows every $Q_q,E_q$ sends zero objects to zero objects, and hence zero morphisms to zero morphisms. Define $v_{q,A}=\eta^0_{Q_{q+1}(A)}\pi_{q,A}:E_q(A)\to E_{q+1}(A)$; the displayed equations make $v_q$ natural.

source.place: Tag 0141 (lemma-functorial-injective-resolutions), proof, recursive cokernel construction; omitted functoriality verification

proof.text: For each object $A$, the augmented sequence $0\to A\xrightarrow{\eta^0_A}E_0(A)\xrightarrow{v_0}E_1(A)\xrightarrow{v_1}\cdots$ is exact. Indeed $\pi_{q+1,A}\eta^0_{Q_{q+1}(A)}=0$, giving $v_{q+1}v_q=0$. Since $\eta^0_{Q_{q+1}(A)}$ is monic, $\ker v_q=\ker\pi_{q,A}=\operatorname{im}\eta^0_{Q_q(A)}$; for $q>0$ this is $\operatorname{im}v_{q-1}$ since $\pi_{q-1,A}$ is epic. For $q=0$ it is the image of $A$. These are the kernel/cokernel properties of [def-sp-abelian]. All $E_q(A)$ are injective by Step 2.

source.place: Tag 0141 (lemma-functorial-injective-resolutions), proof, exactness of the augmented columns

proof.text: For an integer-indexed complex $K$ of [def-weil-abstract-derived-category], form $D_K^{q,p}=E_q(K^p)$ for $q\ge0$, extending by zero for $q<0$. The first differential is $v_{q,K^p}$ and the second is $E_q(d_K^p)$. The second squares to zero because $E_q$ preserves composition and zero morphisms; the first squares to zero by Step 4; they commute by naturality of $v_q$. A chain map $f:K\to L$ gives $D_f^{q,p}=E_q(f^p)$, commuting with both differentials by functoriality and naturality. The maps $\eta^0_{K^p}:K^p\to D_K^{0,p}$ commute with the second differential and are killed by the first differential. If $K^p=0$ for $p<a$, every $D_K^{q,p}$ is zero for $p<a$ by Step 3. This proves each required bicomplex identity directly, without choosing $a$ in the construction.

source.place: Tag 0141 (lemma-functorial-injective-resolutions), proof, construction of the double complex, with indices exchanged

proof.text: Define $I(K)^n=\bigoplus_{q+p=n}D_K^{q,p}$ and use the total differential $v+(-1)^q E_q(d_K)$ of [def-sp-double-complex-total], extending its formula to these integer indices. Existence needs only finite biproducts of [def-sp-abelian]: for any lower bound $a$ the only nonzero terms lie at $0\le q\le n-a$, so their finite biproduct is a coproduct of the entire diagonal by assigning zero maps from the omitted zero objects. Choose a coproduct of this entire diagonal for each $K,n$; the universal property defines $I(f)$ uniquely from the components $E_q(f^p)$, so identity and composition follow by checking coprojections. The differential squares to zero: the two mixed terms have coefficients $(-1)^{q+1}$ and $(-1)^q$ and cancel. On the summand $D_K^{q,p}$ the resolution components of $d_{I(L)}I(f)$ and $I(f)d_{I(K)}$ agree because $v_{q,L^p}E_q(f^p)=E_{q+1}(f^p)v_{q,K^p}$. Their complex components agree because $E_q(d_L^p)E_q(f^p)=E_q(f^{p+1})E_q(d_K^p)$, and both carry the coefficient $(-1)^q$. Equality on every coprojection therefore proves that $I(f)$ is a chain map. Let $\alpha_K^n$ be $\eta^0_{K^n}$ followed by the $(0,n)$ inclusion. Its first differential is zero, and the second has sign $+1$ there, so $\alpha_K$ is a chain map. Naturality follows from $E_0(f^n)\eta^0_{K^n}=\eta^0_{L^n}f^n$ and the defining equation of $I(f)$ on that inclusion.

source.place: Tag 0141 (lemma-functorial-injective-resolutions), proof, associated total complex and the omitted functoriality verification

proof.text: To prove $\alpha_K$ is a quasi-isomorphism, choose a lower bound $a$ only for this verification, and set $A^r=K^{a+r}$ and $B^{q,r}=D_K^{q,a+r}$ for $q,r\ge0$. These form a first-quadrant bicomplex, with augmentation $A\to B^{0,\bullet}$. Step 5 verifies its chain-map equation and annihilation by the first differential. Step 4 shows that for every $r$ the resolution column $B^{\bullet,r}$ has cohomology $A^r$ in degree zero and zero in positive degrees; thus its augmented single-object map is a quasi-isomorphism. The map $b:A\to\operatorname{Tot}(B)$ is exactly the augmentation followed by the $(0,r)$ inclusion and is a chain map by Step 6. Apply [lem-sc-first-quadrant-column-augmentation], whose hypotheses are precisely these, to obtain that $b$ is a quasi-isomorphism. Reindex degree $m$ of its total to degree $a+m$ of $I(K)$: the diagonal bijection $(q,r)\mapsto(q,a+r)$ gives a canonical isomorphism of the chosen coproducts by their universal properties. Its components are identities on the matching summands, so it commutes with both differentials, including the unchanged sign $(-1)^q$, and takes $b$ to $\alpha_K$. These chain isomorphisms induce isomorphisms of kernels and images and hence of cohomology in the relabelled degrees, proving the claim in all degrees $n\ge a$. In degrees $n<a$ both complexes are zero, so their cohomology is zero as well.

source.place: Tag 0141 (lemma-functorial-injective-resolutions), proof, application of Homology Tag 0133 (lemma-double-complex-gives-resolution), via its first-quadrant variant

proof.text: Every $I(K)^n$ is injective: it is a finite biproduct of the injective objects $E_q(K^p)$. For a monomorphism $M\to N$ and a map into this biproduct, extend each of its finitely many component maps using [def-sp-injective-resolutions] and assemble the extensions by the biproduct universal property. The empty biproduct is zero and is injective by the same lifting definition. For every lower bound $a$ of $K$, no pair $q\ge0$, $p\ge a$ has $q+p=n<a$, so $I(K)^n=0$ below $a$. The functors $Q_q,E_q$, the entire-diagonal coproduct choices and their morphisms were fixed before using a lower bound; $a$ enters only the proofs of finite support and quasi-isomorphism. Thus there is one functor $I$ and one natural transformation $\alpha$, valid for every bound. For any diagram $F$ of bounded-below complexes, compose with $I$; the naturality equality proved in Step 6 supplies the augmentation of diagrams, without a common bound for all objects.
